doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 1 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: Touring America with the big bands and playing for dancers
summary: He describes seeing the country, meeting people, dance audiences and listeners, and fans who knew the records note for note.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Can you give — we have a student sitting watching this tape — can you give him an idea of what it was like to be in a large group, and crisscrossing the country at that time?

Well it was interesting to me because having just come out of school I had a lot of interest in geography, which now I began to see laid out before me. That made it interesting. And you know seeing people, meeting people in different states and finding out that most of us think the same way and that we have the same ideas about what the country is and what the world is to a great extent. And this of course kind of reinforced your own thoughts. I found that interesting. And the reaction of people to what you were playing was nice too, that was very encouraging.
Would you have a certain group of people in front of the stage perhaps that just wanted to watch?

We had that. People who came, the aficionados who just came to listen and decide whom they liked best in the band and things of that type, and others were out there dancing the whole time you know. But there was always interest in listening to what we were playing, for all the bands.
It’s so fascinating to think that at that time the music you were playing is like the rock ‘n roll of today. It was the popular music.

At that time it was, yes it was, it was quite popular. And another thing, people listened to a lot of your recordings so that when you went to a town to play, if you had a few recordings out they had listened to them and they knew every note, certainly of the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

ensemble playing you know, and some of the solos, if you repeated them the same way each time, they could hum them note for — or sing them note for note you know. That was true with Benny Goodman and all the big bands at that time.
